00Orientation

How this book works

Four parts: how Spring thinks, building REST APIs, working with data, and running in production. Every annotation is explained by what it makes Spring do behind your back.

The Ramu Chai franchise kit

Ramu's chai is so popular that he sells franchises. A new owner gets a kit: a stove already fitted (embedded Tomcat), a manager who hires staff and tells each one who they work with (the IoC container), standard recipes that work out of the box but can be changed (auto-configuration), a front-desk host who sends each customer to the right counter (DispatcherServlet), and a security guard at the door (Spring Security). The owner only writes what's special about their branch.

Spring Boot 4 note

This book is written for Spring Boot 4.x (Spring Framework 7, Java 17–25, Jakarta EE 11), while pointing out where Boot 3 differs, since many companies still run 3.x. The full list of changes is in Chapter 24. Java concepts this book builds on (proxies, ThreadLocal, thread pools) are in Java Core · Chapter 20 and nearby chapters.

01Foundations

What are Spring and Spring Boot?

Spring is the framework (IoC, DI, AOP, MVC, data, security). Spring Boot is the opinionated starter kit on top: auto-configuration, starters and an embedded server, so you can run with java -jar.

The franchise kit

Plain Spring is a warehouse of excellent kitchen equipment: you choose every part, wire the gas, plumb the sink and write the manual yourself. Spring Boot is the franchise kit: the same equipment, pre-assembled with sensible defaults, plug in and start serving. You can still swap any part.

FeatureSpring FrameworkSpring Boot
ConfigurationManual (Java config or XML)Auto-configuration, overridable
SetupComplex: pick and align versionsStarters with managed, compatible versions
ServerExternal Tomcat/Jetty; deploy a WAREmbedded Tomcat (default) or Jetty; run a JAR
MonitoringManualActuator built in
GoalFull controlConvention over configuration
Lock it in

Spring = the equipment. Boot = the kit, assembled.

Boot = auto-configuration + starters + embedded server + production features. Opinionated defaults, overridable anytime. Non-web apps work too (spring.main.web-application-type=none, CommandLineRunner).

Interview questions

What is "convention over configuration"?

The framework assumes sensible defaults (port 8080, Jackson for JSON, Hikari for connection pooling, component scanning from the main package) so you only configure what differs from the convention.

What are the advantages of an embedded server?

The app is a single self-contained JAR: same artifact in every environment, no server installation or WAR deployment, easy containerisation (one process per container), and server settings live in application properties.

Next: Architecture and the request journey →
02Foundations

Architecture: the life of an HTTP request

Filters → DispatcherServlet → handler mapping → controller → service → repository → database, and back through message converters as JSON. Each layer has one job.

In the franchise

A customer walks in. The guard checks them (filters). The host at the front desk reads their order and sends them to the right counter (DispatcherServlet). The counter clerk takes the order (controller), the chef decides how to make it (service), the storekeeper fetches ingredients (repository) from the storeroom (database). The finished cup goes back along the same path.

LiveFollow GET /api/orders/7 through Spring MVC
LayerAnnotationResponsibilityMust not
Controller@RestControllerHTTP: map URLs, bind/validate input, choose status codescontain business rules or SQL
Service@Servicebusiness logic, transactions, orchestrationknow about HTTP (no HttpServletRequest)
Repository@Repositorydata access; translates SQL exceptions to Spring's DataAccessExceptioncontain business decisions
Entity / DTO@Entity / recordtable mapping / API shapebe mixed up (separate types)
Lock it in

Guard, host, clerk, chef, storekeeper.

Filters → DispatcherServlet (front controller) → HandlerMapping → controller → service → repository. Keep controllers thin.

Interview questions

What is the DispatcherServlet and why is it called the front controller?

It's the single servlet that receives every request to Spring MVC. It looks up the handler through HandlerMappings, invokes it through a HandlerAdapter (resolving arguments), handles exceptions via HandlerExceptionResolvers, and writes the result with message converters or view resolvers. One entry point that delegates is the Front Controller pattern.

Filter vs HandlerInterceptor?

Filters are servlet-level and run before the DispatcherServlet for every request (security, CORS, compression). Interceptors are Spring MVC-level, run around controller methods, and know which handler was chosen (auditing, per-endpoint timing, locale).

Next: IoC container and dependency injection →
03Foundations

IoC container and dependency injection

Inversion of Control: your classes stop creating their own collaborators. The container creates every bean and injects what each one needs.

In the franchise

Without a manager, the chef would have to hire his own storekeeper, and if the storekeeper changes, the chef's job description changes too (tight coupling). With a manager, the chef just says "I need a storekeeper". The manager hires everyone, introduces them, and replaces anyone when needed, even with a stand-in for training day (a mock in tests).

Three ways to inject

recommended
Constructor

Dependencies are final and mandatory, the object is never half-built, cycles fail fast, and tests just call new.

optional deps
Setter

For truly optional or re-configurable dependencies. The object can exist without them.

avoid
Field (@Autowired on a field)

Hidden dependencies, can't be final, needs reflection or Spring to test. Common in old code and tutorials.

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

BeanFactoryApplicationContext
WhatBasic container: create and wire beansBeanFactory + events, i18n messages, resource loading, environment/profiles, AOP integration
Singletons createdLazily, on first requestEagerly at startup (fail fast on config errors)
Used byAlmost nobody directlySpring Boot (e.g. AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext)
Circular dependencies

A needs B and B needs A. Since Boot 2.6 circular references are prohibited by default, and with constructor injection they fail at startup with "The dependencies of some of the beans form a cycle". The right fix is a redesign: extract the shared logic into a third bean, or use events. @Lazy on one constructor parameter is a workaround, not a fix.

Lock it in

Don't hire your own staff. Ask the manager.

IoC = container controls object creation. DI = it hands you dependencies. Constructor injection, depend on interfaces.

Interview questions

IoC vs DI?

IoC is the principle: control over creating and wiring objects moves from your code to a framework. DI is the technique Spring uses to implement it: dependencies are passed in (constructor, setter or field) instead of looked up or created.

Why is constructor injection preferred?

Immutability (final fields), required dependencies are obvious and guaranteed, no partially constructed objects, easy unit testing without a container, and circular dependencies surface immediately. Too many constructor parameters is a useful smell that the class does too much.

Next: Bean lifecycle and scopes →
04Foundations

Bean lifecycle and scopes

Instantiate → inject → aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessors before → init (@PostConstruct) → BeanPostProcessors after (proxies!) → ready → @PreDestroy. Singleton is the default scope.

In the franchise

A new staff member is hired (instantiated), given their tools and colleagues' names (dependencies injected), told the branch name (Aware callbacks), sent to orientation (@PostConstruct), maybe given an assistant who answers on their behalf (a proxy added by a BeanPostProcessor), and then starts work. On closing day they hand back their keys (@PreDestroy).

LiveBean lifecycle stepper: watch OrderService being born

Scopes

ScopeOne instance per…Typical use
singleton (default)container (not per JVM, not per class)stateless services, repositories, controllers
prototypeevery injection or getBean()stateful helpers, builders
requestHTTP requestper-request context
sessionHTTP sessionshopping cart in server-rendered apps
applicationServletContextrare
websocketWebSocket sessionchat state
Singletons are shared by all threads

A singleton service handles every request concurrently. Never keep per-request state in its fields (private User currentUser; is a data leak between customers). Keep services stateless, or use thread-safe structures. See Java Core · Chapter 18.

Lock it in

Hire, equip, orient, assist, work, retire.

Constructor → injection → Aware → BPP before → @PostConstruct → BPP after (proxy) → ready → @PreDestroy. Prototype beans never get @PreDestroy.

Interview questions

What is a BeanPostProcessor?

A hook that sees every bean before and after initialisation and can modify or replace it. Spring uses them to apply AOP: the after-init step wraps beans with @Transactional, @Async or @Cacheable in proxies. That's why the object injected into others is often a proxy, not your class.

Is a singleton bean thread-safe?

Not automatically. Singleton means one instance per container; many request threads call it at once. It's safe if it's stateless (only final, thread-safe dependencies). Mutable fields need synchronization or should be moved to method locals.

Why isn't @PreDestroy called on prototype beans?

The container hands prototype instances to the caller and doesn't track them afterwards, so it can't know when they're done. The caller must clean them up.

Next: Core annotations and component scan →
05Foundations

Core annotations, component scan and choosing between beans

Stereotypes mark classes as beans; component scan finds them from the main package down; @Primary and @Qualifier break ties when two beans fit.

In the franchise

Staff wear badges: Chef, Cashier, Storekeeper (stereotypes). On day one the manager walks through the branch and every room inside it collecting everyone with a badge (component scan from the main package). If two people can make tea, the manager either names a default tea-maker (@Primary) or the chef asks for one by name (@Qualifier).

AnnotationMeaningExtra behaviour
@Componentgeneric Spring-managed beannone
@Servicebusiness logic layernone (documents intent)
@Repositorydata access layertranslates persistence exceptions into DataAccessException
@ControllerMVC controller returning viewshandler detection
@RestController@Controller + @ResponseBodyreturn values are written as JSON
@Configuration + @BeanJava config: factory methodsCGLIB proxy so inter-@Bean calls return the same singleton
AnnotationPurpose

Lock it in

Badges, a walk through the building, a default, or a name.

@Component for your classes, @Bean for third-party ones. Scan starts at the main class's package. @Primary = default, @Qualifier = explicit.

Interview questions

@Component vs @Bean?

@Component is on a class and is detected by component scanning. @Bean is on a method inside a @Configuration class and you construct the object yourself; use it for third-party classes, or when creation needs logic or conditions.

What does @SpringBootApplication contain?

@SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan (from the annotated class's package).

Why is @Configuration proxied?

So that one @Bean method calling another returns the container's singleton instead of creating a new object. Spring subclasses the config class with CGLIB and intercepts those calls. @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) skips the proxy for faster startup when methods don't call each other.

Next: Auto-configuration and starters →
06Foundations

Auto-configuration and starters: how Boot "just knows"

Boot reads a list of candidate configuration classes and keeps only those whose @Conditional checks pass: is this class on the classpath, is that bean missing, is this property set?

In the franchise

The kit has a rule book: "If the shop has a gas line, fit a gas stove. If the owner already brought their own stove, don't fit ours. If the owner ticked 'serve coffee', install the coffee machine." The installer reads the rules on opening day and fits only what applies. That's auto-configuration.

LiveCondition evaluator: change the classpath and your own beans, see what Boot configures

Starters

Starter (Boot 4 name)Brings
spring-boot-starter-webmvc (was -web)Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat, Jackson 3
spring-boot-starter-data-jpaSpring Data JPA, Hibernate 7, HikariCP
spring-boot-starter-securitySpring Security 7
spring-boot-starter-validationJakarta Bean Validation (Hibernate Validator)
spring-boot-starter-actuatorhealth, metrics, Micrometer
spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test, -data-jpa-test…Boot 4 splits test support per technology (JUnit 6, Mockito, AssertJ)
Lock it in

If there's gas, fit a stove, unless the owner brought one.

Imports file → @ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingBean / OnProperty → beans. Your bean wins. --debug shows why.

Interview questions

How does auto-configuration work internally?

@EnableAutoConfiguration imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which loads candidate classes from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports in every jar (spring.factories before Boot 2.7/3). Each candidate is a @Configuration guarded by @Conditional annotations evaluated against the classpath, existing beans, properties and environment. Matching ones register their beans, after user configuration, so @ConditionalOnMissingBean lets user beans take precedence.

How would you write your own starter?

Create an autoconfigure module with an @AutoConfiguration class (conditions + @ConfigurationProperties), list it in the AutoConfiguration.imports file, and a starter module that depends on it plus the libraries. Name it acme-spring-boot-starter (only Spring's own starters use the spring-boot-starter-* prefix).

Next: Configuration, properties and profiles →
07Foundations

Configuration, properties and profiles

Same JAR, different settings per environment. Properties come from many sources with a clear precedence; bind groups of them into typed objects with @ConfigurationProperties.

In the franchise

Every branch gets the same kit, but the Kolkata branch sets the price list in rupees and opens at 6 am, while the airport branch opens 24 hours. The settings live on a card pinned inside the door (properties), not welded into the stove. A note from head office on the day (command-line argument) beats the card.

Where values come from (highest priority first)

  1. Command-line argumentsjava -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
  2. Environment variablesSERVER_PORT=9090, SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=… (relaxed binding: dots → underscores, upper case). The usual way in Docker/Kubernetes.
  3. Profile-specific filesapplication-prod.yml when spring.profiles.active=prod
  4. application.properties / application.ymlin src/main/resources (or ./config/ next to the JAR, which wins over the packaged one)
  5. Defaultsin code: @Value("${x:default}"), field initialisers in properties classes.
Secrets

Never commit passwords or API keys in properties files. Inject them as environment variables from a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault, Kubernetes Secrets). See Cloud & DevOps · Chapter 16.

Lock it in

Same kit, a different card on each door.

Command line > env vars > profile file > application file > defaults. @ConfigurationProperties for groups, @Value for one-offs. Profiles: spring.profiles.active.

Interview questions

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@Value injects single values with SpEL support but no grouping, validation or metadata. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix to a typed object (records work well) with relaxed binding, validation, conversion (Duration, DataSize), IDE autocompletion via the configuration processor, and one place to see all settings.

How do you manage config across dev, test and prod?

One artifact; profile-specific files or blocks for non-secret differences; environment variables or a config server / secrets manager for secrets and per-environment values; ddl-auto none/validate in prod with Flyway or Liquibase migrations.

08REST APIs

REST API basics: resources, methods and status codes

URLs name things (nouns), HTTP methods say what to do (verbs), status codes say what happened. Every request carries everything the server needs: stateless.

In the franchise

The menu board lists things: /orders, /orders/7. What you do with them is the verb: look (GET), place a new order (POST), replace your whole order (PUT), change only the sugar (PATCH), cancel (DELETE). The counter answers with a token colour: green "here you go" (200), "order placed" (201), red "we don't have that" (404).

POSTcreatePOST /api/orders201 + Locationnono
PUTreplace whole resourcePUT /api/orders/7200 / 204yesno
PATCHpartial updatePATCH /api/orders/7200not guaranteedno
DELETEremoveDELETE /api/orders/7204yesno
2xx
Success

200 OK · 201 Created · 202 Accepted (async) · 204 No Content

@RequestParamquery string / form field/orders?status=PAID
@RequestBodyrequest body (JSON → object){"item":"chai","qty":2}

Interview tip: design checklist

Plural nouns (/orders), nesting only for ownership (/orders/7/items), pagination on every list, an Idempotency-Key header for POSTs that move money, versioning (/api/v1 or a header; Boot 4 has built-in API versioning, see Chapter 24), and a consistent error format (RFC 9457 ProblemDetail, Chapter 12).

Lock it in

Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method, outcome in the status.

GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. 201 + Location for create, 204 for delete. 401 = who are you, 403 = not allowed.

Interview questions

PUT vs PATCH vs POST?

POST creates a new resource (server picks the id) and isn't idempotent. PUT replaces the full resource at a known URL; repeating it gives the same state. PATCH applies a partial change; it can be idempotent (set status = PAID) or not (add 1 item), depending on the patch.

What makes an API RESTful?

Resources identified by URIs, a uniform interface (standard methods and status codes), stateless requests, cacheable responses where appropriate, client–server separation and layered systems. HATEOAS (links in responses) is the strict final constraint, rarely used in practice.

09REST APIs

Your first CRUD API, end to end

Project structure → dependencies → entity → repository → service → controller → properties → run → test with curl. Type this once and you'll understand every later chapter.

In the franchise

Ramu's first digital project: a student register for his chai-making school. Add a student, list them, look one up, update, remove. Five endpoints, four classes, one database table.

LivePractice terminal: run the app and call every endpoint
Lock it in

Entity, repository, service, controller, properties, curl.

Three core deps: starter-webmvc, starter-data-jpa, a DB driver. Main class at the root package. Run 4 ways: IDE, mvn spring-boot:run, gradle bootRun, java -jar.

Interview questions

Why didn't update() call save()?

Inside a transaction, entities loaded by Hibernate are managed. On commit Hibernate compares them with the snapshot taken at load time (dirty checking) and issues the UPDATE automatically. save() on a managed entity is harmless but redundant.

What is a fat JAR?

An executable JAR built by the Spring Boot Maven/Gradle plugin that nests your classes, all dependency JARs and a launcher, so java -jar app.jar starts the app with its embedded server. For containers, Boot can also extract it into layers for better Docker caching.

Next: DTOs, mapping and Lombok →
10REST APIs

DTOs, mapping and Lombok

Never send entities over the wire. A DTO is the API's contract; the entity is the database's. Keep them separate and map between them.

In the franchise

The kitchen's stock register has supplier prices, margins and staff notes. The customer gets a printed menu with just names and prices. You'd never hand customers the stock register, and you can rearrange the kitchen without reprinting menus.

Security leaks

Serialising an entity exposes password hashes, internal flags and audit columns, and lets clients set fields they shouldn't (mass assignment).

Lazy-loading surprises

Jackson touches lazy collections: LazyInitializationException, N+1 queries, or infinite recursion between parent and child.

Coupled contract

Renaming a column changes your public API and breaks mobile apps.

Lombok: less boilerplate, with care

AnnotationGeneratesOn JPA entities?
@Getter / @Setteraccessorsfine
@NoArgsConstructor(access = PROTECTED)the constructor JPA needsfine
@RequiredArgsConstructorconstructor for final fields (great for DI)for services
@Builderfluent builderwith care
@Slf4jprivate static final Logger logfor services
@Datagetters, setters, equals, hashCode, toStringavoid: equals/hashCode on mutable ids, toString touches lazy relations
Modern Java

Records already give you immutable DTOs with constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString, so for DTOs you rarely need Lombok at all. Jackson 3 (in Boot 4) binds records out of the box.

Lock it in

Stock register stays in the kitchen; customers get the menu.

Request DTO in, response DTO out, entity in the middle. Records for DTOs, MapStruct for big mappings, no @Data on entities.

Interview questions

Why are records a good fit for DTOs?

They're immutable, concise, have value-based equals/hashCode/toString, work with Bean Validation annotations on components, and serialise/deserialise with Jackson without extra configuration.

How do you avoid infinite recursion when serialising bidirectional relationships?

Best: return DTOs that don't contain back-references. Workarounds on entities: @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference or @JsonIgnore on one side.

Next: Validation →
11REST APIs

Validation: reject bad input at the door

Annotate the DTO, put @Valid on the parameter, and Spring returns 400 before your code runs. Custom rules are an annotation plus a validator class.

In the franchise

The order form has rules printed on it: name required, phone must be 10 digits, quantity 1 to 20. The clerk checks the form at the counter and hands it back with the wrong boxes circled; the chef never sees an invalid order.

Constraintnull""" "Use for
@NotNull✗✓✓any type
@NotEmpty✗✗✓strings, collections, maps, arrays
@NotBlank✗✗✗strings (strictest)

Also: @Size, @Min/@Max, @Positive, @Email, @Pattern, @Past/@Future, @Digits, @DecimalMin.

Common trap

Validation annotations alone do nothing: without @Valid (or @Validated on the class for method parameters) they're never checked. And validate DTOs at the API boundary; business rules that need the database (email already exists) belong in the service.

Lock it in

Rules on the form, check at the counter.

@NotNull ⊂ @NotEmpty ⊂ @NotBlank. @Valid on @RequestBody, @Validated for path/query params. Custom = @Constraint + ConstraintValidator.

Interview questions

@Valid vs @Validated?

@Valid is the standard Jakarta annotation: triggers validation of an argument and cascades into nested objects. @Validated is Spring's: on a class it enables method-level validation of simple parameters via a proxy, and it supports validation groups.

What are validation groups?

Marker interfaces assigned to constraints so different rules apply in different contexts, e.g. id must be null on Create but not null on Update: @Validated(OnCreate.class).

Next: Exception handling and ProblemDetail →
12REST APIs

Exception handling: one place, one error format

Throw meaningful exceptions from the service; translate them to HTTP once, in a @RestControllerAdvice. Use RFC 9457 ProblemDetail as the response body.

In the franchise

When something goes wrong, the chef doesn't run to the customer. He sends a slip to the complaints desk, which has a standard apology card for each problem: "out of stock", "card declined", "kitchen closed". Customers always get the same, polite format, never the chef's shouting.

Common trap

Returning stack traces or SQL error text to clients leaks internals and helps attackers. Log the details with a correlation/trace id; return a clean message containing that id.

Lock it in

One complaints desk, one apology card format.

Throw domain exceptions → @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler → ProblemDetail. Specific handlers first, Exception.class last.

Interview questions

@ControllerAdvice vs @RestControllerAdvice?

@RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody, so handler return values are written as the response body (JSON) rather than resolved as view names. Both apply globally (optionally narrowed by package or annotation).

@ResponseStatus on an exception vs @ExceptionHandler?

@ResponseStatus on the exception class maps it to a status with no body customisation. @ExceptionHandler gives full control over status, headers and body, and keeps HTTP knowledge out of domain exceptions. ResponseStatusException is a quick inline option.

Next: Calling other services: RestClient and HTTP interfaces →
13REST APIs

Calling other services: RestClient and HTTP interfaces

RestClient is the modern synchronous client; @HttpExchange interfaces let Spring generate the client for you. Always set timeouts.

In the franchise

The branch orders milk from a dairy by phone. Old way: dial, read out every detail yourself (RestTemplate). New way: a pre-printed order pad with the dairy's fields; fill in quantity and the system places the call (HTTP interface). And never wait on hold forever: hang up after 2 seconds (timeouts).

ClientStyleStatus
RestTemplatesynchronous, template methodsmaintenance mode; fine in old code
RestClient (6.1+)synchronous, fluentdefault choice for servlet apps
WebClientreactive, non-blockingfor WebFlux apps
@HttpExchange interfacedeclarative, generatedFeign-like, built in; Boot 4 adds @ImportHttpServices
OpenFeigndeclarative (Spring Cloud)still common in microservices
Production checklist

Timeouts (connect + read) on every client, retries only for idempotent calls with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker (Resilience4j, or Spring Framework 7's built-in @Retryable/@ConcurrencyLimit resilience annotations), and propagate the trace id. Patterns are explained in System Design · Chapter 13.

Lock it in

A pre-printed order pad, and hang up after two seconds.

RestClient for imperative code, WebClient for reactive, @HttpExchange interfaces for declarative clients. Always timeouts.

Interview questions

RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient?

RestTemplate: older synchronous API, now in maintenance. WebClient: reactive and non-blocking, returns Mono/Flux, best in WebFlux. RestClient: synchronous with a fluent API like WebClient but no reactive dependency; the recommended choice for Spring MVC apps (and fits virtual threads well).

How do services call each other in a microservice architecture?

Synchronously over HTTP/gRPC (RestClient, HTTP interfaces, Feign) when the caller needs an immediate answer, or asynchronously via events on Kafka/RabbitMQ for decoupling and resilience. Add service discovery or Kubernetes DNS, timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.

14Data

JPA and Hibernate: entities, relationships and the N+1 problem

JPA is the specification, Hibernate the implementation, Spring Data the convenience layer. Map classes to tables, keep associations LAZY, and fetch what you need explicitly.

In the franchise

The storekeeper keeps a working copy of every ledger page he's opened today (the persistence context). Change a number on his copy and he updates the real ledger at closing time (dirty checking on commit). If you ask for 50 customers and then, one by one, "what did this customer order?", he walks to the storeroom 51 times (N+1). Smart: "give me the 50 customers with their orders" in one trip (JOIN FETCH).

RelationshipExampleDefault fetchAdvice
@ManyToOneOrder → CustomerEAGERset LAZY
@OneToOneUser → ProfileEAGERset LAZY; share the PK with @MapsId
@OneToManyOrder → LinesLAZYalways mappedBy (bidirectional) or @JoinColumn
@ManyToManyStudent ↔ CourseLAZYuse Set; often better as an explicit join entity

The N+1 problem

Two traps

JOIN FETCH of a collection + pagination: Hibernate paginates in memory (warning HHH90003004). Page the parent ids first, then fetch. LazyInitializationException: touching a lazy field after the transaction closed. Fix by fetching what you need inside the service, not by turning on EAGER or open-in-view.

Entity states and the persistence context

transient
new, unknown

new Order(): not tracked, no id yet.

managed
tracked

After persist/find inside a transaction: changes are flushed automatically (dirty checking). First-level cache: the same id returns the same object.

detached
was tracked

After the transaction/session ends. Changes are ignored unless you merge.

removed
scheduled for delete

DELETE runs at flush/commit.

ddl-autoDoesWhere
nonenothingproduction (with Flyway/Liquibase)
validatechecks the schema matches; fails on startup if notproduction safety net
updateadds missing tables/columns, never dropslocal dev only
create / create-dropdrop and recreate (and drop on shutdown)tests, demos
Lock it in

One trip with everything, not fifty-one trips.

JPA = spec, Hibernate = implementation. LAZY everywhere, fetch explicitly (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, DTO projections). Owning side has the FK; mappedBy marks the inverse. Prod: ddl-auto none/validate.

Interview questions

What is the N+1 problem and how do you detect it?

One query loads N parents, then accessing a lazy association triggers one query per parent. Detect with SQL logging (spring.jpa.show-sql or a datasource proxy), Hibernate statistics, APM traces showing repeated identical queries, or tests asserting query counts. Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or DTO projections.

What is the first-level cache?

The persistence context (EntityManager/Session) caches entities by id for the duration of the transaction, so repeated find calls return the same instance without a query and changes are tracked for dirty checking. A second-level cache (Ehcache, Caffeine via JCache) is optional and shared across sessions.

What does cascade = ALL with orphanRemoval do?

Cascade propagates persist/merge/remove from parent to children. orphanRemoval deletes a child row when it's removed from the parent's collection. Use only for true composition (order lines belong to one order), never on @ManyToOne.

Next: Spring Data repositories and queries →
15Data

Spring Data repositories: queries from method names

Declare an interface; Spring generates the implementation at startup. Method names become queries; @Query covers the rest; Pageable keeps lists bounded.

In the franchise

The storekeeper understands a fixed phrasebook: "find by name", "count by city", "find by price between … order by name". Say it in that form and he knows exactly which shelf to check. For anything unusual you hand him a written note (@Query).

KeywordSQL
And / OrWHERE a AND/OR b
GreaterThan, LessThanEqual, Between>, <=, BETWEEN
Like, Containing, StartingWithLIKE with wildcards
In, NotIn, IsNull, TrueIN (…), IS NULL, = true
OrderBy…Desc, First/Top10, DistinctORDER BY, LIMIT, DISTINCT
Deep pages

OFFSET 100000 makes the database read and discard 100,000 rows. For infinite scroll or exports use keyset (cursor) pagination: WHERE id < :lastSeenId ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 (Spring Data supports it with ScrollPosition / Window).

Lock it in

Speak the phrasebook; hand over a note when you can't.

Derived methods for simple queries, @Query when the name gets long, @Modifying for updates, projections for read APIs, Pageable on every list.

Interview questions

save() vs saveAndFlush()? findById vs getReferenceById?

save() persists or merges and the SQL runs at flush/commit; saveAndFlush() forces the SQL immediately (useful to catch constraint violations now). findById queries and returns an Optional; getReferenceById returns a lazy proxy without a query (great for setting a foreign key: order.setCustomer(repo.getReferenceById(id))), throwing EntityNotFoundException only if accessed and missing.

Page vs Slice?

Page runs an extra COUNT query to know total elements/pages. Slice only fetches size+1 rows to know whether there's a next page: cheaper for "load more" UIs.

Next: Transactions and @Transactional →
16Data

Transactions: how @Transactional really works

A proxy opens a transaction before your method and commits or rolls back after it. Know the defaults: rollback on unchecked only, REQUIRED propagation, and no effect on self-invocation.

In the franchise

A customer pays and gets chai: both or neither. If the milk runs out after the payment, the cashier refunds (rollback). The manager's assistant (the proxy) stands at the door of every "@Transactional" room: opens the cash drawer when you walk in, closes it when you leave happily, refunds everything if you leave shouting. But if you walk from one room to another through the inside corridor (calling a method in the same class), the assistant never sees you.

LivePropagation explorer: an outer method calls an inner one. What happens?
PropagationIf a transaction existsIf none exists
REQUIRED (default)join itstart one
REQUIRES_NEWsuspend it, start a new independent onestart one
NESTEDsavepoint inside it (JDBC only)start one
SUPPORTSjoin itrun without
MANDATORYjoin itthrow
NOT_SUPPORTEDsuspend it, run withoutrun without
NEVERthrowrun without

The gotchas that appear in every interview

readOnly = true
For queries

Hibernate skips dirty checking and snapshots (less memory/CPU), and some drivers/routers send it to a read replica. Put it on the class, override on writes.

isolation
How much you see of others

READ_COMMITTED (Postgres default), REPEATABLE_READ (MySQL InnoDB default), SERIALIZABLE. See System Design · Chapter 5.

timeout
Fail fast

timeout = 5 seconds: rolls back long-running transactions.

keep it short
No HTTP calls inside

A transaction holds a DB connection. Calling a slow API inside it exhausts the pool. Call out first, or use the outbox pattern.

Lock it in

The assistant guards the door, not the corridor.

Proxy-based: public methods, called from another bean. Rolls back on unchecked only. REQUIRED joins, REQUIRES_NEW suspends and starts fresh. Keep transactions short.

Interview questions

How does @Transactional work internally?

At startup a BeanPostProcessor wraps beans having @Transactional in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy for interfaces or CGLIB subclass). On each call the TransactionInterceptor asks the PlatformTransactionManager (JpaTransactionManager) to begin or join a transaction based on propagation, binds the connection/EntityManager to the current thread (ThreadLocal), invokes the real method, then commits or rolls back according to the rollback rules.

REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW, with a real use case.

REQUIRED joins the caller's transaction: if anything fails, everything rolls back together. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller and runs independently: its commit survives the caller's rollback. Use case: write an audit log or a "payment attempted" record that must persist even if the main business transaction rolls back. Beware: it uses a second connection.

Inner REQUIRED method throws, outer catches the exception. What happens?

The inner proxy marks the shared transaction rollback-only. The outer method continues, but on commit Spring finds it rollback-only and throws UnexpectedRollbackException; nothing is saved. Use REQUIRES_NEW (or NESTED) for the inner call if its failure should be isolated.

Next: Production data: locking, migrations, pools →
17Data

Production data: concurrency control, migrations and connection pools

Two users editing the same row need a locking strategy; schemas change through versioned migrations; and the connection pool is usually your real concurrency limit.

In the franchise

Two clerks both see "1 samosa left" and both sell it. Ramu's fix: each tray has a version sticker; you can only take from it if the sticker hasn't changed since you looked (optimistic locking). For the last cylinder of gas, he simply holds the key until he's done (pessimistic locking).

Schema migrations with Flyway

HikariCP: the pool everyone forgets

Lock it in

Version sticker for rare clashes, hold the key for hot items.

@Version = optimistic, FOR UPDATE = pessimistic. Flyway versioned migrations. Pool size × instances ≤ DB limit; keep transactions short; open-in-view off.

Interview questions

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when to use which?

Optimistic (@Version): no DB locks, detects conflicting updates at commit; best for low-contention data and long user think-time; requires retry/409 handling. Pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE): blocks competing transactions; best for short, high-contention operations like inventory decrements or wallet debits; risk of waits and deadlocks, so lock in consistent order with timeouts.

What is spring.jpa.open-in-view and why disable it?

Open Session in View keeps the Hibernate session (and a DB connection) open until the HTTP response is rendered, so lazy loading works in controllers and Jackson. It hides N+1 queries and holds connections longer under load. Boot warns about it; disable it and fetch needed data in the service.

18Production

Spring Security: the filter chain, JWT and method security

Every request passes through a chain of security filters before it reaches your controller. Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you may do.

In the franchise

At the door, the guard checks your membership card (authentication). A signed wristband from the front desk lets you walk around without showing ID again (a JWT). Some rooms need a staff badge (role ADMIN) and the kitchen checks it again at the kitchen door (method security). The guard never keeps a list of who's inside: the wristband itself proves it (stateless).

LiveJWT login and an authenticated request, step by step
Session cookieJWT bearer token
Stateserver stores the session (or Redis)stateless: token carries the claims
Scalingsticky sessions or shared session storeany instance can verify
Logout / revokedelete the session: instanthard: short expiry + refresh tokens + denylist
CSRFneeds CSRF protectionnot needed if not stored in cookies
Best forserver-rendered web appsmobile apps, SPAs, service-to-service
Common traps

Putting secrets in the JWT payload (it's only Base64, anyone can read it). Long-lived access tokens with no revocation. Accepting alg: none or not checking expiry (use the library, don't parse by hand). Storing passwords with MD5/SHA-256 instead of a slow, salted hash (BCrypt, Argon2). Forgetting that role checks need the ROLE_ prefix with hasRole.

Lock it in

Card at the door, wristband after, badge for staff rooms.

SecurityFilterChain bean, deny by default, STATELESS + CSRF off for token APIs, BCrypt, oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(), @PreAuthorize for ownership rules. 401 vs 403.

Interview questions

Explain the Spring Security filter chain.

Spring registers one servlet filter (DelegatingFilterProxy → FilterChainProxy) that delegates to the first matching SecurityFilterChain bean, an ordered list of filters: CORS, CSRF, authentication filters (form, basic, bearer token), exception translation (turns AuthenticationException into 401 and AccessDeniedException into 403), and the AuthorizationFilter that applies the URL rules. The authenticated user lives in the SecurityContextHolder for the request.

How do you implement JWT authentication?

Login endpoint authenticates via AuthenticationManager and issues a signed short-lived access token (and refresh token). Each request's Bearer token is validated by the resource server support (signature, expiry, issuer, audience) which builds the Authentication with authorities from claims. Stateless session policy, HTTPS, key rotation, refresh token rotation and revocation strategy. Prefer an identity provider (Keycloak, Cognito, Auth0) for issuing tokens.

Why BCrypt?

It's deliberately slow with a configurable cost factor and a per-password salt, so brute-forcing leaked hashes is expensive and rainbow tables are useless. The delegating encoder stores the algorithm id ({bcrypt}…) so you can upgrade to Argon2 later.

Next: AOP and proxies: Spring's hidden assistant →
19Production

AOP and proxies: the hidden assistant behind the annotations

@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize and @Retryable all work the same way: Spring wraps your bean in a proxy that runs extra code around the method. Understand the proxy and you understand all their gotchas.

In the franchise

Busy chefs get a personal assistant who stands in front of them. Customers talk to the assistant, who logs the order, checks the card, starts the timer, passes the request to the chef, and stops the timer after. The chef only cooks. But when the chef talks to himself ("now I'll also make the sauce"), the assistant isn't involved: no log, no timer.

Proxy typeHowWhenLimits
JDK dynamic proxyimplements the bean's interfacesbean has interfaces and proxyTargetClass=falseonly interface methods
CGLIB (Boot default)generates a subclass at runtimedefault in Spring Bootcan't proxy final classes/methods or private methods
AnnotationAdvice the proxy adds
@Transactionalbegin / commit / rollback
@Asyncsubmit the call to a TaskExecutor, return immediately
@Cacheablelook up the cache, skip the method on a hit
@PreAuthorizeevaluate the SpEL rule, throw AccessDenied
@Retryable (Framework 7 core)re-invoke on failure with backoff
@Validatedvalidate method parameters
Lock it in

Talk to the assistant, not to yourself.

Annotation magic = proxy + advice. Proxies only see calls from outside, on public, non-final methods. Fix self-invocation by moving the method to another bean.

Interview questions

What is AOP and where does Spring use it?

Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns (transactions, security, caching, logging, metrics, retries) from business code. Spring AOP implements it with runtime proxies around beans; Spring's own @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable and method security are built on it.

Spring AOP vs AspectJ?

Spring AOP is proxy-based, method-execution join points only, on Spring beans, woven at runtime: simple and enough for most needs. AspectJ weaves bytecode at compile or load time and supports fields, constructors, self-invocation and non-Spring objects, at the cost of build/agent setup.

Next: Caching, async, scheduling and events →
20Production

Caching, async, scheduling and events

Four annotations that remove plumbing: @Cacheable skips repeat work, @Async runs it on another thread, @Scheduled runs it on a timer, and application events decouple who-did-what from who-reacts.

In the franchise

The price of masala chai rarely changes, so the clerk keeps it on a sticky note instead of asking the owner every time (cache), and replaces the note when the price changes (evict). Sending the customer an SMS receipt is handed to a runner so the queue keeps moving (async). Every night at 2 am someone counts the stock (scheduled). When an order is paid, a bell rings and whoever cares reacts: kitchen, loyalty desk, accounts (events).

Same proxy rules

All four rely on proxies: self-invocation skips them, private methods are ignored. Plus: @Async loses the caller's ThreadLocals (SecurityContext, MDC, transaction), so pass what you need as arguments; a void @Async method's exception is only logged unless you configure an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler; @Cacheable keys must be stable and values serialisable for Redis.

Lock it in

Sticky note, runner, night shift, a bell.

@Cacheable skips on hit, @CachePut refreshes, @CacheEvict removes, always a TTL. @Async on a bounded pool. Cron = sec min hour day month weekday. AFTER_COMMIT listeners for side effects.

Interview questions

How do you keep a cache consistent with the database?

Cache-aside with TTL: read through @Cacheable, evict (not update) on writes after commit, keep TTLs short for changing data. Accept brief staleness, or for critical data skip caching. Beware stampedes on hot keys (Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite, locking or request coalescing). Details in the System Design book's caching chapter.

A @Scheduled job runs on every pod. How do you run it once?

Use a distributed lock (ShedLock with a DB/Redis lock table), a leader election, a dedicated single-replica worker deployment, or move it out to a platform scheduler (Kubernetes CronJob, Cloud Scheduler, EventBridge) that calls an endpoint or runs a job.

Actuator, logging and observability

Actuator exposes health, metrics and runtime info; Micrometer sends metrics and traces to your monitoring stack; structured logs tie it together.

In the franchise

Head office can't visit every branch, so each kitchen has a status board by the door: gas OK, fridge OK, 42 orders/hour, average wait 3 min (health + metrics). Each order slip carries a tracking number so a complaint can be traced from counter to kitchen to delivery (trace id).

Only health is exposed by default. Separate management port, liveness/readiness probes, Prometheus metrics, structured logs with trace ids. DevTools is dev-only.

Interview questions

How do you change a log level in production without restarting?

POST to /actuator/loggers/com.ramu.orders with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"} (secured endpoint), or via a config server refresh. Revert afterwards.

Liveness vs readiness probes?

Liveness: is the process healthy or should Kubernetes restart it (don't include downstream dependencies, or a DB outage restarts every pod). Readiness: can it take traffic now (warming up, draining during shutdown, critical dependency down); failing it removes the pod from the Service without restarting.

22Production

Testing: unit, slice and integration tests

Many fast unit tests, some slice tests that load one layer, a few full integration tests with real dependencies in containers.

In the franchise

Taste each ingredient alone (unit tests: quick, cheap, many). Test the counter with a pretend kitchen behind it (slice test with mocks). Once a week, run a full rehearsal with real gas and real milk (integration test with Testcontainers).

Test typeLoadsSpeedUse for
Plain JUnit + Mockitonothingmsservice logic
@WebMvcTest(X.class)MVC for one controller, advice, filters~1 sstatus codes, JSON, validation, security rules
@DataJpaTestJPA, repositories, a test DB; rolls back each test~2 squeries, mappings

Lock it in

Taste ingredients, test the counter, rehearse once a week.

Unit → slice (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) → @SpringBootTest. @MockitoBean replaces beans in the context (Boot 4); @Mock is plain Mockito. Real DBs via Testcontainers, not H2.

Interview questions

@Mock vs @MockitoBean (@MockBean)?

@Mock creates a Mockito mock with no Spring involvement (unit tests). @MockitoBean (Spring Framework 6.2+; replaces Boot's @MockBean, removed in Boot 4) creates a mock and puts it into the Spring ApplicationContext in place of the real bean, for slice and integration tests. Each distinct set of mocked beans creates a new cached context, so keep them consistent.

Why Testcontainers instead of H2 for repository tests?

H2 behaves differently from PostgreSQL/MySQL (SQL dialect, JSON types, locking, constraints), so tests pass and production fails. Testcontainers runs the real database version in Docker, and @ServiceConnection removes the connection boilerplate.

23Production

Microservices with Spring Boot and Spring Cloud

One service = one business capability = one database. A gateway in front, discovery (or Kubernetes DNS) between them, resilience on every call, events for decoupling, tracing across all.

In the franchise

Ramu's head office splits into separate counters with their own stock: Orders, Payments, Kitchen, Loyalty. A receptionist (API gateway) greets every visitor and sends them to the right counter. Counters talk by intercom for quick questions (REST) and by a notice board for announcements (Kafka). If Loyalty's line is busy, Orders doesn't wait forever (circuit breaker).

ConcernSpring optionOn Kubernetes, often
API gatewaySpring Cloud GatewayIngress / Gateway API, cloud API gateway
Service discoveryEureka, ConsulKubernetes Services + DNS
ConfigurationSpring Cloud ConfigConfigMaps, Secrets, cloud secret managers
Service callsRestClient / HTTP interfaces / OpenFeignsame, plus a service mesh
ResilienceResilience4j (circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, rate limiter)plus mesh retries/timeouts
MessagingSpring for Apache Kafka, Spring AMQP, Spring Cloud Streammanaged Kafka (MSK, Confluent), Pub/Sub
TracingMicrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetryTempo, Jaeger, X-Ray, Cloud Trace
Distributed data

No shared database, so no cross-service @Transactional. Use the transactional outbox (write the event in the same DB transaction, relay it to Kafka) and sagas with compensating actions. Full explanation with diagrams: System Design · Chapter 14 and System Design · Chapter 11.

Lock it in

Separate counters, one receptionist, intercom and a notice board.

Database per service, gateway in front, timeouts + circuit breakers on sync calls, idempotent consumers on async ones, outbox + saga instead of distributed transactions, tracing everywhere. Start with a modular monolith.

Interview questions

How does a circuit breaker work?

It wraps calls and counts failures over a sliding window. CLOSED: calls pass. When the failure rate crosses a threshold it goes OPEN: calls fail fast to the fallback without hitting the sick service. After a wait it goes HALF_OPEN and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it, failure re-opens. It stops cascading failures and thread-pool exhaustion.

When would you not use microservices?

Small teams, unclear domain boundaries, early-stage products, or when you can't invest in CI/CD, observability and on-call for many services. A well-modularised monolith is faster to build and can be split later along proven boundaries.

Next: What's new in Spring Boot 4 →
24Production

What's new in Spring Boot 4 (and 4.1)

Boot 4.0 (November 2025) is a generational release on Spring Framework 7: modular auto-configuration, Jackson 3, JSpecify null-safety, API versioning, HTTP service clients, and removal of everything deprecated in 3.x.

In the franchise

Every few years Ramu redesigns the franchise kit. The new one is lighter (you only ship the parts you use), the labels are stricter (null-safety), the old phone-order forms are gone (deprecated APIs removed), and it fits the newest stoves (Java 25).

AreaWhat changedWhat you do

Modularisationauto-configuration split into focused modules; starters renamed: -web → -webmvc; per-technology test startersswitch starter names (old ones still resolve, deprecated)
JSONJackson 3: packages tools.jackson.*, unchecked JacksonException, JsonMapperBuilderCustomizerupdate imports and customizers
Null safetyJSpecify @Nullable/@NullMarked across the portfoliobetter IDE/Kotlin null checks

RemovedUndertow support; everything deprecated in 3.xTomcat or Jetty
4.1 (June 2026)Spring gRPC integration, lazy JDBC connection acquisition, SSRF protection for clients, @RedisListeneropt in as needed
Interview tip

If asked "what's new?", pick three: modular starters (smaller apps, faster startup), Jackson 3 + JSpecify (safer code, a real migration step), and first-class API versioning + HTTP service clients (less custom code). Then say how you'd migrate: OpenRewrite recipes, the properties migrator module, and a staged rollout. Also good to know: Spring AI 2.0 is built on Boot 4 (see AI Engineering · Chapter 16).

Lock it in

Lighter kit, stricter labels, old forms gone.

Boot 4 = Framework 7, Java 17–25, Jakarta EE 11, Jackson 3, modular starters, API versioning, @MockitoBean, no Undertow.

Interview questions

How would you migrate a Boot 2.7 service to Boot 4?

In steps: Java 17+, then Boot 3.x (javax → jakarta, Security 6 config style, Hibernate 6) using OpenRewrite; then the latest 3.5 with zero deprecation warnings; then 4.0 (starter renames, Jackson 3 imports, @MockitoBean, test package moves, removed properties via spring-boot-properties-migrator). Rely on a good integration test suite and deploy canary first.
